title: New Associate Hiring is Flat — Is AI The Cause?
author: Artificial Lawyer

dom.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-reconfiguration and entry-level competence-risk framing, then adds specific AmLaw 200 evidence: junior hiring stayed flat while lateral hiring and firm revenues grew. It treats AI as a plausible contributor rather than established cause, noting that the pattern predates widespread legal-AI use, and materially extends the practical response by urging faster junior development as AI absorbs entry-level tasks.
qs: The trend toward flat newbie hiring started *before* widescale legal AI use.

The data also underlines – AL would argue – the need for law firms to train up junior lawyers more rapidly, so they can deliver more valuable work product, especially as AI chews up the entry-level tasks.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI is removing entry-level tasks that traditionally developed junior lawyers and that firms must respond with more deliberate, accelerated training. It treats AI as only one plausible contributor to flat hiring, however, and does not substantively address the verification paradox or specify simulation, mentorship and independent-practice methods.

kp.k: Entry-level AmLaw 200 hiring remained broadly flat
kp.d: SurePoint’s Law School Hiring Report 2026 is cited as showing 7,489 new associates hired in 2022, 7,640 in 2023, 7,417 in 2024 and 7,426 in 2025. The article characterises this as broadly flat, with a small overall decline, despite strong AmLaw 200 market growth; it treats 2021 as a post-Covid outlier.
qs: Data from SurePoint’s Law School Hiring Report 2026 found that in the four previous years the number of new associates hired into AmLaw 200 firms, i.e. entry-level joiners from law school, went as follows:
I.e. generally flat, with a small decline overall, at a time when the AmLaw 200 have seen tremendous growth and a very busy few years.
Note that 2021 was an outlier caused by a sudden surge in hiring following Covid in 2020.

kp.k: Revenue growth diverged from new-associate hiring
kp.d: The article estimates that AmLaw 200 firms added several tens of billions of dollars in combined revenue during 2022–2025 while entry-level hiring stayed flat or declined. It frames this as counter-intuitive because conventional firm growth would ordinarily increase demand for junior lawyers.
qs: It’s estimated that during those four years the AmLaw 200 added several tens of billions of dollars in combined revenues, yet as seen above, the number of newbies in the US stayed flat, or dropped.
That seems counter-intuitive, as a growing market would normally demand more entry-level attorneys to ‘feed the engine’.

kp.k: Lateral hiring increasingly exceeded entry-level recruitment
kp.d: The article reports that hiring of experienced lateral associates increased over the three years preceding publication, following a post-Covid surge and short decline. In 2025, firms hired more lateral associates than entry-level lawyers, indicating a shift toward experienced recruits.
qs: Meanwhile, the number of lateral associate hires, i.e. more experienced lawyers who are hired from other law firms, rose over the last three years after an initial surge and a short drop after Covid.
In fact, last year in 2025, there were more laterals than newbies.

kp.k: AI may now contribute to flat junior hiring
kp.d: The author says legal AI previously lacked sufficient adoption or meaningful use to affect hiring materially, but suggests that by 2025 many firms were probably deploying AI at scale and that adoption would broaden in 2026. AI is therefore presented as a plausible contributing factor, not an established causal explanation; the article explicitly says its magnitude and future effects remain unknown.
qs: In previous years this site would have said ‘no’. Why? Because legal AI uptake was just not broad enough, or its use meaningful enough, to have much of an impact.
Yet, many firms by 2025 probably were using AI tools at scale, and in 2026 many more will be.
Therefore, it seems reasonable now to suggest that AI is playing into these figures*.
The challenge is we don’t know how much yet, or where this is heading.

kp.k: Client AI use may reduce outsourced junior tasks
kp.d: The article proposes a potential double impact: law firms use AI internally, while clients use AI for routine work that might otherwise have been outsourced to AmLaw 200 juniors. This is offered as a possible mechanism rather than a measured finding.
qs: At the same time, many clients are also using AI for routine tasks – some of which would have been sent out to the junior lawyers at AmLaw 200 firms.
So, potentially a double impact.

kp.k: The hiring trend predates widespread legal AI
kp.d: The author qualifies the AI explanation by observing that flat entry-level hiring began before widespread legal AI adoption. The chronology implies that AI cannot by itself explain the entire four-year pattern and motivates consideration of other market forces.
qs: There is however, another challenge.
The trend toward flat newbie hiring started *before* widescale legal AI use.
So, what else is happening?

kp.k: Clients may resist paying for inexperienced lawyers
kp.d: As one speculative non-AI explanation, the author suggests clients have become more reluctant to pay for work performed by very inexperienced associates. No direct client evidence or quantified effect is supplied in the article.
qs: AL’s guess would be that regardless of AI, some of the below factors may be in play:
Clients are becoming more reticent about paying for very inexperienced lawyers.

kp.k: Profit incentives may favour experienced lateral associates
kp.d: The author speculates that firms seeking higher profits may prefer lateral associates because experienced lawyers can command higher billing rates and require less training before undertaking complex billable work. This is presented as a possible explanation, not an empirically isolated cause.
qs: That law firms – in the search for higher profits – prefer laterals, as more experienced lawyers can be charged out at higher rates, and need less training to do complex billable work.

kp.k: In-house growth may remove basic outsourced matters
kp.d: The article suggests that clients may be expanding their in-house legal teams and using available technology to retain more work, independently of AI. Keeping basic matters in-house could disproportionately reduce the work traditionally allocated to the most junior law-firm associates.
qs: That some clients are growing their own teams – and using whatever tech is available to them – to keep more work inhouse (regardless of AI).
That can tend to reduce the need for law firms to handle their most basic matters – which tend to filter down to the most junior lawyers.

kp.k: Combined forces may increasingly favour lateral hiring
kp.d: Looking ahead, the author predicts that client resistance, firm profit incentives, in-house work retention and greater AI use could combine to strengthen conditions favouring lateral associates over entry-level hires. This is expressly framed as the author’s estimate rather than a demonstrated forecast.
qs: Overall, AL would estimate that these potential trends, added to greater AI use, will combine further in the years to come to create even more powerful conditions that favour laterals over newbies.

kp.k: Firms should accelerate junior lawyer training
kp.d: The article recommends that law firms train junior lawyers more rapidly so they can produce higher-value work as AI absorbs entry-level tasks. The proposed response is faster professional development rather than simply preserving routine junior assignments.
qs: The data also underlines – AL would argue – the need for law firms to train up junior lawyers more rapidly, so they can deliver more valuable work product, especially as AI chews up the entry-level tasks.

kp.k: Persistent divergence would signal structural labour-market dislocation
kp.d: The author cautions that a four-year trend can reverse, but argues that continued AmLaw growth without increased new-lawyer hiring would indicate a deep-seated separation between revenue growth and entry-level employment. AI is predicted to exacerbate, rather than necessarily originate, that trend.
qs: Last word: even a four-year pattern can suddenly shift again.
Trends are just that….trends, and they can tilt in new directions.
But, if this trend did stay in place, while AmLaw firms kept growing, **this would suggest a deep-seated dislocation between revenue growth and new lawyer hiring. **
And, as noted, it would seem reasonable to suggest that AI will only exacerbate such a trend.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer tentatively attributes part of flat US entry-level associate hiring to AI and predicts that AI, alongside other pressures, will increasingly favour experienced lateral hires over new graduates.
pts.d: The author proposes a potential double impact: law firms' own AI use may reduce demand for entry-level work, while clients' use of AI for routine tasks may reduce work sent to firms' juniors. Artificial Lawyer does not claim that AI explains the entire hiring pattern or quantify its contribution. It predicts that greater AI use combined with client resistance to paying for inexperienced lawyers, firms' preference for higher-rate and less training-intensive laterals, and clients keeping more work in-house will further favour laterals. The author also argues that firms need to train juniors more rapidly for higher-value work as AI takes over entry-level tasks. If flat entry-level hiring persists alongside firm growth, the author sees a possible structural separation between revenue growth and new-lawyer hiring that AI could intensify.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The empirical basis is SurePoint's hiring data; the AI explanation is Artificial Lawyer's interpretation rather than a measured causal finding.
pts.d: The article cites SurePoint’s Law School Hiring Report 2026 for AmLaw 200 entry-level hires: 7,489 in 2022, 7,640 in 2023, 7,417 in 2024 and 7,426 in 2025. It contrasts this broadly flat series with an estimate that combined firm revenues increased by several tens of billions of dollars over those four years, without specifying the basis for that revenue estimate. It also reports that lateral hiring rose over the last three years and exceeded entry-level hiring in 2025, without providing lateral counts. Assertions about scaled AI adoption and clients using AI are not accompanied by adoption measurements or direct evidence linking AI to hiring decisions. The author explicitly presents alternative explanations as guesses and acknowledges that the hiring trend predates widespread legal AI use.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The observed hiring period is 2022–2025; the proposed AI contribution becomes plausible to the author around 2025–2026, with further effects predicted over unspecified coming years.
pts.d: Writing in 2026, Artificial Lawyer says it previously would not have attributed the pattern to AI because adoption and meaningful use were insufficient. It now estimates that many firms probably used AI at scale by 2025 and expects more to do so in 2026. The prediction that laterals will be favoured applies to the coming years and assumes the combination of rising AI use and other proposed pressures. The stronger claim of a deep-seated separation between revenue growth and entry-level hiring is explicitly conditional on continued flat hiring and continued AmLaw growth. The author cautions that a four-year pattern can reverse and notes that 2021 was an exceptional post-Covid hiring surge.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern US AmLaw 200 firms, their entry-level and lateral associates, and corporate clients retaining routine work internally.
pts.d: New law-school graduates face potentially constrained hiring demand despite growing firm revenues, and junior associates face reduced entry-level task opportunities and pressure to develop higher-value capabilities faster. Experienced lateral associates are predicted to become relatively more attractive to firms. AmLaw 200 firms may grow without proportionate increases in new-graduate hiring and face a need to accelerate junior training. Clients and their in-house teams are described as retaining work through AI and other technology, reducing external demand for basic matters. The article's evidence concerns entry-level hiring, not measured layoffs or total legal employment.
